decisions.0: Ace-jack suited opens from under the gun every time: it is one of the stronger hands even with five players still to act.
decisions.1: On six-five-four the big blind's range is slightly ahead of yours, and your ace-high has two overcards but nothing made. A bet would fold the hands you beat and get called mostly by pairs and draws. Checking takes a free card and keeps the pot small; small bets are only slightly worse, and checking is the natural play here.
decisions.2: The nine misses you. Your ace-high still beats the big blind's king-high hands and some weaker aces, so it can win at showdown; a bet would fold exactly those hands and get called by pairs. Checking keeps that showdown value; betting three quarters of the pot costs 0.42 bb.
decisions.3: The two means any three makes a straight. After the big blind checks, your ace-high still wins against its king-high hands and weaker aces, which is why your equity is 60.9%. Those hands will not call a bet, though, so a bet gets called mainly by better hands; checking wins at showdown, and betting half the pot costs 0.23 bb.

takeaway: Ace-high can be a showdown hand: when a bet would only be called by better, check and let it win at showdown.
